transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. [name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. Um... I guess what finally pushed me to come in is that I just... I can’t seem to organize the moving parts anymore. There's just so much going on—patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, team decisions at work. 

Actually, the gallery thing is sort of a new side project. My sister-in-law runs this little art space downtown, right next to where that old Italian place used to be? The one that closed a couple of years ago, which is a real shame because they had this amazing mushroom risotto. I actually tried to recreate it at home a few weeks ago, but I got completely sidetracked looking for the right kind of arborio rice online and ended up burning the shallots. My whole kitchen smelled like smoke for two days. 

But, um, anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the moving parts. With the software team and the patents and everything else, I just... I end up starting whatever is loudest, you know? Like whatever is screaming for my attention right in that exact second, instead of what actually matters. I just can't seem to keep it all straight anymore.
Would you say you've struggled with this kind of scattered attention and difficulty organizing tasks since you were a child, or is this something that's really only become a problem recently?

Yeah, um, looking back... it was definitely there in grade school, too. It's not just a recent thing. My teachers used to write on my report cards that I was bright, but that I daydreamed a lot. 

I would actually do the work—like, I’d have the finished assignments sitting right there in my backpack, and I’d just completely forget to turn them in. Or I'd lose my homework folders entirely. I had this one really specific folder in fourth grade, it was a Trapper Keeper with this neon laser grid on it, very eighties. I got it at this stationary store that used to be in the old mall. Man, that mall is completely dead now. They turned the main anchor store into a massive indoor trampoline park, which is a neat idea for utilizing the space, I guess, but the parking is just atrocious now. I tried taking my nephew there last month and we had to park like three blocks away, and it was raining. 

But, um... wait, sorry. What was I saying? Oh, right, the folders. Yeah, long before I was even a teenager, I was already losing my homework folders and spacing out in class. So I guess it's always been there.

Have you ever gone through a distinct stretch of days or weeks where you felt unusually energetic, elated, or irritable—needing much less sleep than usual and feeling like your mind was racing more than normal—that was different from how you feel most of the time?

No, I don't think so. I mean, my mind is always kind of racing, but not in a way where I feel super elated or energetic, you know? It's more just... crowded. Like a browser with fifty tabs open and I don't know which one is playing music. 

Speaking of browsers, we just rolled out this huge update at work that completely changed how our internal dashboard interfaces with the main database. It was supposed to streamline everything, but honestly, it’s been a nightmare. The UI is so clunky now. It reminds me of this old desktop computer my dad bought us in the nineties. It had this massive CRT monitor that took up half the desk, and we had to use dial-up to get online. The sound of that modem connecting... it's permanently burned into my brain. *Eee-err-eee-err*. We used to get kicked off whenever someone picked up the phone in the kitchen. My mom was always on the phone with my Aunt Carol, who lived in Florida and grew these giant grapefruits. She’d send us a box every Christmas, and they were so sour you had to pour sugar all over them just to eat them.

But, um... wait, what did you ask me? Something about sleep? Oh, right. No, I don't get those weird stretches of feeling super energetic or anything. I just feel overwhelmed most of the time.

When your mind feels crowded like that, is it mostly filled with worried thoughts about things that might go wrong, or is it more that your attention keeps jumping between unrelated things without a particular sense of worry?

It's not really worry, no. I mean, I worry about getting fired because I'm behind, but the thoughts themselves aren't usually anxious. It's more just... bouncing around. Like, if I'm in the middle of coding something and Slack pings, or even if just a browser tab flashes in the background, I'm completely derailed. Or sometimes it's not even an external thing—I'll just get a visual idea for the gallery space popping into my head, and suddenly I've lost the thread of what I was supposed to be doing. I'll spend twenty minutes going down some completely unrelated design rabbit hole. 

Actually, speaking of rabbit holes, I fell down a massive one the other night looking up the history of neon signs. Because I was thinking about that laser grid on my old folder, right? And I wondered how they actually made neon back in the day. Turns out, it's this incredibly delicate glass-bending process. They have to heat the glass tubes over these ribbon burners and blow into them to keep them from collapsing while they bend them. It's fascinating. There's this one guy on YouTube who has been doing it for like forty years in this tiny shop in Chicago. He made this huge custom piece for a diner that looked like a giant stack of pancakes with syrup dripping off it. It made me so hungry watching it. I actually ended up ordering pancakes on DoorDash at like midnight, which was a terrible idea because they arrived all soggy. The syrup had completely soaked through the cardboard container. 

But, um... wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right, the worry thing. Yeah, no, it's not usually worry. It's just my attention jumping from one thing to another like that. Slack pings, and boom, I'm gone.

Would you say these attention and organization difficulties are causing significant problems in more than one area of your life—like at work, at home, and in your relationships—or is it mostly limited to one setting?

Yeah, it's definitely bleeding into everything, but work is... work is where it's really blowing up in my face lately. It’s actually starting to seriously damage my reputation there. Like, I completely missed this major patent filing checkpoint recently. Which was a huge deal because the legal team had been setting up all these prep meetings. 

The main patent attorney we use, he has this insane Zoom background filled with vintage cuckoo clocks. Like, wall-to-wall clocks. I made the mistake of asking him about it once while we were waiting for others to join, and he went on this massive tangent about the Black Forest clockmakers in the 1700s. Did you know they used to carve all the internal gears entirely out of wood because brass was too expensive? Just sitting in these tiny snowed-in cabins in Germany, whittling tiny little gears. It actually made me want to try woodworking. I ended up buying a lathe on Craigslist a few years ago, thinking I'd make bowls or something, but it's still sitting in my garage. It's right next to an elliptical machine I also never use, which my wife is always on my case about. Our garage is basically just a graveyard for my good intentions at this point. She can't even park her car in there anymore. 

But, um... sorry, I lost the thread again. What were you asking? Oh, right, if it affects multiple areas. Yeah, so home is a mess with the garage and stuff, but missing that patent thing at work was really bad. And then we had this really difficult architecture review right after, and I was just totally scattered during the presentation. It went so poorly that it left the other collaborators actively questioning whether I can even lead the larger project moving forward. So, yeah, it's definitely causing significant problems in a few places, but the work stuff is what's really scaring me right now.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports chronic, pervasive inattentive symptoms (distractibility, losing materials, forgetting to turn in completed work, difficulty organizing tasks, tangential/disorganized thought pattern) beginning in childhood ('grade school,' 'long before I was even a teenager') and persisting into adulthood, causing significant functional impairment across multiple domains (work performance/reputation, home organization, relational strain). No evidence of manic/hypomanic episodes (denies elevated mood, decreased sleep need, or racing thoughts tied to euphoria) ruling out bipolar spectrum, and the intrusive thoughts are not anxious/worry-based, arguing against a primary anxiety disorder. The pattern of tangential, distractible speech itself during the interview is consistent with inattentive-type ADHD rather than psychotic or mood-driven flight of ideas. This supports a diagnosis of Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, predominantly inattentive type (F90.0).
